key_terms.meaning: The set of all points in space that the wave has reached with the same phase; for a distant source it is a plane.
A line drawn perpendicular to the wavefront; it shows the direction in which light energy travels.
The line drawn perpendicular to the boundary surface at the point where the ray strikes it.
n = c/v, where c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light in vacuum and v is its speed in the medium.
n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r, with i the angle to the normal in medium 1 and r the angle in medium 2.
Two sources that keep a constant phase difference, so their waves give a steady interference pattern.
Δ = the extra distance one wave travels compared with the other before they meet, in metres.
Δ = mλ, m = 0, 1, 2, …; the two waves arrive in phase and add.
Δ = (2m + 1)λ/2; the two waves arrive in opposite phase and cancel.
β = λD/d, the spacing between two neighbouring bright fringes, with D the slit-to-screen distance and d the slit separation.
β = λ/(2θ), where θ is the small angle between the two glass plates, in radians.
r<sub>m</sub> = √(mλR) for the m-th dark ring in reflected light, R being the radius of curvature of the lens.
An instrument that splits one beam by a half-silvered plate, sends the two parts along two arms and recombines them.
One fringe crossing the field means the movable mirror has moved λ/2; N fringes mean d = Nλ/2.
A film of thickness t = λ/(4μ) and index μ = √(n<sub>s</sub>) makes the two reflected waves cancel on a substrate of index n<sub>s</sub>.
The bending of light around edges and through narrow openings, caused by the superposition of the wavelets from one wavefront.
(a + b) sin θ = mλ, where (a + b) is the slit spacing, θ the angle of the m-th maximum and λ the wavelength.
R = λ/Δλ = mN, with m the order and N the total number of illuminated slits.
tan θ<sub>p</sub> = n; at this angle of incidence the reflected light is completely plane polarized.
I = I₀ cos²θ, giving the light intensity I passing through an analyser at angle θ to the polarizer.

takeaways: At any boundary a light wave splits into a reflected part and a refracted part, and the angles obey the law of reflection and Snell's law.
Two coherent waves added point by point give a steady pattern of bright and dark fringes fixed by their path difference.
In a thin film the reflected waves carry a path difference of about 2μt cos r, plus a half-wave loss when reflection happens at a denser medium.
An air wedge converts fringe counting into a ruler: each fringe stands for a thickness change of λ/2.
Newton's rings measure the radius of curvature of a lens from the ring radii, because r<sub>m</sub>² grows linearly with the ring number.
A Michelson interferometer turns mirror movement into a fringe count, with each fringe equal to λ/2 of travel.
A quarter-wave anti-reflection coating cancels reflection by making the two reflected waves equal in amplitude and opposite in phase.
A grating spreads different wavelengths to different angles through (a + b) sin θ = mλ, which is how a spectrometer reads wavelength.
Light is a transverse wave, so its electric field has a direction; a polarizer selects one direction and Malus's law gives the transmitted intensity.
bank_note: Long answers here are mostly derivations with a diagram: fringe width, air wedge, Newton's rings, the grating equation and the quarter-wave coating, each followed by one practical measurement or application.

bank.q: Define a wavefront and a ray. Using Huygens' construction at a plane boundary, prove the law of reflection and Snell's law, and explain how the incident energy splits between the reflected and refracted waves.
outline: Wavefront: locus of points with the same phase; the ray is normal to it.
Each point on the boundary acts as a source of secondary wavelets.
Reflection: the triangles for incident and reflected wavefronts are congruent, so i = r.
Refraction: the same wavefront spans the boundary in the same time, giving sin i / sin r = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂.
The split of energy depends on n₁ and n₂; at normal incidence the reflected fraction is ((n₂ − n₁)/(n₂ + n₁))².

bank.q: State the conditions for sustained interference of light. Derive the expression for fringe width in Young's double-slit experiment and explain what happens to the pattern when the whole apparatus is dipped in water.
outline: Needs coherent sources, equal or comparable amplitudes, and the same plane of polarization.
Path difference at a point on the screen: Δ = xd/D.
Bright when Δ = mλ, dark when Δ = (2m + 1)λ/2.
Fringe width β = λD/d.
In water λ falls to λ/n, so the fringes become n times narrower and the pattern shrinks.

bank.q: Derive the conditions for brightness and darkness in the light reflected from a thin transparent film of thickness t and refractive index μ. Explain the half-wave loss and show how the result leads to an anti-reflection coating.
outline: Optical path difference between the two reflected rays: 2μt cos r.
Extra λ/2 appears because one reflection is at a denser medium.
Bright: 2μt cos r = (2m + 1)λ/2; dark: 2μt cos r = mλ.
For normal incidence and a film one quarter wave thick, 2μt = λ/2, giving cancellation.
Equal reflected amplitudes are also needed, which fixes the coating index.

bank.q: Explain how a quarter-wave film on glass kills reflection. Give the required film thickness and refractive index, and state why the coating works only over a narrow band of wavelengths.
outline: Two reflections: air-film and film-glass, each with a half-wave loss, so the extra phase comes only from the path 2μt.
Set 2μt = λ/2, so t = λ/(4μ).
Set the two reflected amplitudes equal, which gives μ = √(n<sub>s</sub>) for substrate index n<sub>s</sub>.
Both conditions hold exactly at one λ, so away from it the cancellation is partial.
Multilayer stacks widen the band.

bank.q: Explain the polarization of light. State Brewster's law and Malus's law, describe how a Polaroid sheet produces plane polarized light, and give two uses of polarized light.
outline: Light is transverse; the electric field direction defines the state of polarization.
Types: plane, circular and elliptical polarization.
Brewster: tan θ<sub>p</sub> = n, reflected ray then perpendicular to the refracted ray.
Malus: I = I₀ cos²θ through an analyser.
Uses: reducing glare from roads and water, stress analysis in photoelasticity, LCD screens.

bank.q: Describe the air wedge experiment with a neat diagram. Derive β = λ/(2θ) and explain how the wedge measures the thickness of a thin foil or wire.
outline: Two glass plates touching at one edge, separated by a foil at the other, film of air between them.
Thickness at distance x from the contact edge: t = xθ.
Path difference 2t plus λ/2, so dark fringes where 2t = mλ.
Fringe width β = λ/(2θ); consecutive fringes differ in thickness by λ/2.
Measure β over many fringes with a travelling microscope, then t<sub>foil</sub> = Lθ.

bank.q: Describe Newton's rings formed in reflected light. Derive r<sub>m</sub>² = mλR for the m-th dark ring and explain how the radius of curvature of the lens surface is determined.
outline: Plano-convex lens on a flat plate; air film thickness grows with radius.
Geometry: t = r²/(2R) for small r.
Path difference 2t + λ/2; dark when 2t = mλ.
Hence r<sub>m</sub>² = mλR; the square of the radius grows linearly with ring number.
Plot r<sub>m</sub>² against m: slope gives λR, so R = slope/λ.

bank.q: Draw and explain the Michelson interferometer. Show that a mirror movement of λ/2 shifts the pattern by one fringe, and give three applications.
outline: Half-silvered plate splits the beam into two arms; mirrors send them back.
Compensating plate equalises the glass path in both arms.
Optical path difference 2d cos θ; circular fringes.
One fringe equals a path change of λ, hence mirror travel λ/2 per fringe.
Applications: measuring small displacements, refractive index of gases, wavelength comparison, Fourier-transform spectroscopy.

bank.q: Describe a plane transmission grating and derive (a + b) sin θ = mλ. Explain how the wavelength of sodium light is measured with it.
outline: Grating: N parallel slits of width a and opaque spacing b, so the grating element is (a + b).
Path difference between neighbouring slits is (a + b) sin θ; maxima when this equals mλ.
Zero order is white; higher orders separate the wavelengths.
Spectrometer: set the grating normal to the collimator, measure θ on both sides of the direct image.
λ = (a + b) sin θ / m, using the mean of the two angles.

bank.q: In a Michelson interferometer, moving one mirror by 0.030 mm shifts 100 fringes across the field. Find the wavelength. In an air wedge with λ = 589 nm, 30 dark fringes span 1.5 cm; find the wedge angle and the foil thickness at 5 cm from the contact edge.
outline: Fringe width β = 1.5 × 10⁻² m / 30 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Foil thickness at L = 0.05 m: t = Lθ ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻⁵ m = 29 μm.

bank.q: Compare interference and diffraction point by point: origin of the fringes, width of the fringes, intensity distribution, and number of sources involved.
outline: Interference comes from two separate coherent wavefronts; diffraction from the infinite set of wavelets of one wavefront.
Interference fringes are equally spaced and of equal intensity; diffraction fringes are unequal in width and fall off in intensity.
In interference the dark fringes are truly dark; in diffraction the minima are not perfectly dark.
Interference needs two sources; diffraction needs one slit or edge.
Both follow the same superposition rule and the same path-difference conditions.

bank.q: Explain why the centre of Newton's rings is dark in reflected light and bright in transmitted light. Describe the changes when a liquid of refractive index μ is placed between the lens and the plate.
outline: At the centre the film thickness tends to zero, so the only path difference is the half-wave loss on reflection.
Hence reflected light cancels at the centre; in transmitted light the loss occurs once, so the centre is bright.
With liquid of index μ the path becomes 2μt, so rings shrink: r<sub>m</sub>² = mλR/μ.
If μ lies between 1 and the glass index the half-wave loss stays at the liquid-glass surface and the pattern keeps the same form.
Ring size therefore measures the liquid's refractive index.

bank.q: Explain why a grating produces much sharper maxima than two slits. Define resolving power of a grating, derive R = mN, and explain missing orders.
outline: With N slits the amplitude adds N times but the intensity N² times at the maxima, so peaks become sharp and narrow.
Between principal maxima there are N − 1 minima and N − 2 weak secondary maxima.
Resolving power R = λ/Δλ = mN; more slits or higher order resolves closer wavelengths.
Missing orders occur when a diffraction minimum of one slit falls on an interference maximum of the grating.
Condition: (a + b)/a = m/n for integers m and n.

bank.q: A silicon solar cell has refractive index 3.5. Choose a coating material and thickness that minimises reflection at 600 nm. Evaluate how well the same coating performs at 450 nm and at 750 nm, and state what design change would widen the low-reflection band.
outline: Ideal index μ = √3.5 ≈ 1.87; no common material matches exactly, so choose the nearest available and accept partial cancellation.
At 450 nm and 750 nm the optical thickness is no longer λ/4, so the two reflected waves are not in exact antiphase and reflection rises.
Reflection also rises because the two reflected amplitudes are unequal when μ ≠ √n<sub>s</sub>.
A multilayer stack, or a graded-index layer, broadens the band at extra cost.

glossary.def: A surface joining all points of a wave that have the same phase at a given instant.
A line drawn perpendicular to the wavefront, showing the direction of energy flow.
The perpendicular to the boundary at the point of incidence, from which all angles are measured.
The ratio n = c/v of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium.
The relation n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r obeyed by a ray crossing a boundary between two media.
Two sources whose waves keep a constant phase difference, so a steady interference pattern forms.
The product μ × (geometrical distance), the distance the light would cover in vacuum in the same time.
The angle by which one wave leads another, equal to (2π/λ) times the path difference.
A bright or dark band in an interference or diffraction pattern.
The distance between the centres of two neighbouring bright fringes, usually written β.
Interference between the waves reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of a film of thickness comparable to λ.
Two glass plates meeting at a small angle, enclosing a film of air whose thickness increases steadily.
Circular fringes formed by the air film between a plano-convex lens and a flat glass plate.
An instrument that splits a beam into two arms with a half-silvered plate and recombines them to form fringes.
A thin film on a surface, a quarter wavelength thick, that makes reflected waves cancel and so raises transmission.
The spreading of light around obstacles and through narrow slits, from superposition of wavelets of one wavefront.
A plate with a large number of equally spaced parallel slits that disperses light into orders.
The distance (a + b) between the centres of two neighbouring slits, with a the slit width and b the opaque gap.
The ratio λ/Δλ, where Δλ is the smallest wavelength difference the grating can just separate.
The restriction of the electric field of a transverse wave to one direction or to a definite pattern of rotation.
A device that transmits only the component of the electric field along one axis.
The angle of incidence at which the reflected light is completely plane polarized, given by tan θ<sub>p</sub> = n.
The transmitted intensity through an analyser is I = I₀ cos²θ, with θ measured from the polarizer axis.
An extra phase change of π, equivalent to a path change of λ/2, when light reflects from a denser medium.
